text.en: Trisha makes two rectangles. She says, I increased the area of my rectangle, and the perimeter increased. Is that always true? We will explore.

The area of a rectangle = number of squares in one row x number of rows, that is, length x breadth. For a square, side x side.
A rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm has area 40 square cm. A square of side 6 cm has area 36 square cm.
Shapes made of 12 squares can be 6 x 2, 4 x 3 or 12 x 1. All have area 12 square units but perimeters 16, 14 and 26 units. So the same area can give different perimeters.
Shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas. With perimeter 16: 7 x 1 has area 7, 6 x 2 has 12, 5 x 3 has 15 and 4 x 4 has 16.
So is Trisha always right? No. From 12 x 1 (area 12, perimeter 26) to 4 x 4 (area 16, perimeter 16) the area increased but the perimeter decreased.
Area and perimeter are different things: area measures the inside in square units and perimeter measures the border in units of length.
(additional, not in the textbook) For a fixed perimeter, the square gives the biggest area.

problem.en: Find the area and perimeter of a rectangle 8 cm long and 5 cm broad.

why.en: Add length and breadth and double.

prompt.en: Is it true that when the area of a rectangle increases, its perimeter always increases? Explain with an example.

requiredIdeas.en: 4 x 4 has area 16 but perimeter 16, which is smaller

commonMisconceptions.en: Believing bigger area means bigger perimeter

points.en: Area of a rectangle = length x breadth.
Same area can give different perimeters.
Same perimeter can give different areas.
Area is in square units, perimeter in length units.
